scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Goat on the Drum
This is orteke. 19th century.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Orteke's origins extend back to ancient Turkic nomadic communities, with some ethnographers linking early forms to shamanic healing rituals and spirit vessels.
The tradition began spreading more broadly in the 19th century and reached formal institutional stages in the 1930s at the Almaty Puppet Theater.
In 1935, composer Akhmet Kuanovich Zhubanov published a detailed account in Kazachstanskaja pravda.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Orteke celebrates the nomadic love for nature and the observation of wild mountain goats, encapsulated by the imagery of a goat trapped in a pit.

It serves as an important folk heritage marker, an intergenerational communication tool between adults and children, and is showcased at biennial international festivals and regional puppet competitions.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The performance centers on a carved wooden marionette shaped like a mountain goat, positioned on a drum or table covered in skin or embroidered cloth.
A küyshi connects the puppet to their fingers and wrists using fine strings and metal rods.
As they play the dombra, finger movements animate the puppet, which hops and strikes the drumskin.
Watch for mountain goat leap.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The primary musical instrument is the two-stringed dombra (or dombyra), played by a küyshi.
Percussion is generated directly by the dancing puppet striking a dauylpaz drum.
Listen for the dombra, dauylpaz, sazsyrnay, shankobyz.
Rapid plucking of a two-stringed dombra coupled with the sharp, rhythmic percussive taps of a wooden marionette striking a dauylpaz drumskin.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Puppets are traditionally carved from woods including red birch, walnut, maple, ash, and oak, though regional variations like those in Semirechye employed dried mountain goat skin stuffed with straw.
The stage setting consists of a small table or drum surface draped with animal skin or fabric featuring national embroidery.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key historical figures and performers associated with orteke melodies include Küyşi Tattimbet, Bayserke, Şaşubay, Navrızbay, and composer Akhmet Kuanovich Zhubanov.
The tradition is shared across Turkic-nomadic regions.
Orteke is classified as an indigenous Kazakh performing art, a subclass of Kazakh folk dance, and a traditional puppetry-music fusion.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Early ethnographers note that orteke originally functioned as a shamanic tool and spirit vessel during healing rituals before evolving into a secular folk performance.
